passage:
Dear Zainab,
Thanks for listening last night. I know I talked in circles. Let me put it simply.
Raghav and I have been together five months. He's kind. But when things started getting physical, I felt rushed, and I froze instead of saying so. Nothing happened I didn't agree to, but I didn't like freezing.
So on Sunday I told him, calmly: I want to slow down, and I want us to talk before, not after. He was quiet, then said, "Thank you for telling me. I'd hate for you to feel that way."
We also agreed to go to the campus health centre together to talk about protection and testing, like adults.
I feel lighter. Also slightly embarrassed writing this. 😅
Usha

qa.q: Where did Usha and Raghav agree to go together?
qa.a: They agreed to go to the campus health centre.

qa.q: Why did Usha feel uneasy even though nothing happened without Usha's agreement?
qa.a: Usha froze instead of speaking up, so the boundary never got said, and that was unsettling.

qa.q: What made Usha's conversation with Raghav effective?
qa.a: Usha chose a calm moment, stated clearly what was needed, and they planned to get proper health information together.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel after Usha's honesty?
qa.a: He seemed grateful and caring, and may feel more trust in the relationship knowing Usha will tell him how things feel.

grounding: A young adult's letter shows Usha communicating boundaries and planning responsible sexual health care with a partner.

passage: You asked on the show what consent actually looks like in real life. I'm Varun, twenty. Honestly, I used to think it was just about no. Then something happened with my ex, and a friend, Ramesh, who'd trained as a peer educator, sat me down. He asked, "Did you check if she wanted it, or just that she didn't stop you?" That hit hard. I'd never thought about the difference. So now I ask. Out loud. Even when it feels awkward. "Is this okay?" "Want to stop?" And I've learned the answer can change halfway. Ramesh also pushed me to get tested and carry protection, and not treat that as someone else's job. It's less awkward than you'd think. Being unsure is way more awkward.

qa.q: What did Ramesh train as?
qa.a: He trained as a peer educator.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when Ramesh asked his question?
qa.a: It hit him hard, making him realise with some discomfort that he had only been checking for a no, not for a real yes.

qa.q: What habits did Varun build, and why are they responsible?
qa.a: He now asks out loud, accepts that answers can change, gets tested and carries protection, taking his share of responsibility for safety and consent.

qa.q: How might Varun's past partner see his new approach if she heard about it?
qa.a: She might feel it was a lesson learned late, but may be glad he now takes consent seriously.

grounding: A young man describes learning that consent needs a clear yes and taking responsibility for sexual health.

passage: I'm Anirban, and Saurabh has been my flatmate since first year. Last month his girlfriend stayed over after a party. In the morning I heard them talking in the kitchen, more serious than usual. Later Saurabh told me that when they got back from the party, she'd said she'd had too much to drink and didn't want anything to happen, so he'd made her tea and slept on the floor mat. He looked a bit sheepish. "Is that weird?" he asked. I told him no, that's what you do. She thanked him. They're still together. Last week he brought home a leaflet from the student health clinic about safer sex and left it on our shared shelf. He's never been the type to talk about these things, but he seems to take them seriously.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh sleep that night?
qa.a: He slept on the floor mat.

qa.q: Why might Saurabh have looked sheepish when he asked "Is that weird?"
qa.a: He may have worried that friends would tease him for not pursuing more, even though he felt he did the right thing.

qa.q: What did Saurabh get right in this situation?
qa.a: He respected that she'd had too much to drink and didn't want anything, and he cared for her instead of pressuring her.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's girlfriend feel about his choice?
qa.a: She likely felt safe and respected, which helped build trust in the relationship. 🤍

grounding: A flatmate observes a young man respecting consent when his partner has been drinking and taking sexual health seriously.

passage: Monday: Walking back from class, Yamini told Ramesh she wasn't ready to stay over at his flat. He went quiet, kicked a pebble, then said, 'Okay. Thanks for telling me straight instead of making an excuse.' Thursday: On the sofa watching a film while his flatmates were out, he paused before sliding closer. 'This fine?' She nodded, then added that kissing was fine but she wanted to stop there for now. He said, 'Then that's where we stop.' Later they talked, a bit awkwardly, about how any bigger step would come with a real conversation first and proper protection, and how a clinic visit together would not be embarrassing. The next Sunday: Yamini told her roommate she felt safer with Ramesh than with anyone before. 'He asks. And he listens when I answer.'

qa.q: What did Ramesh ask on Thursday before moving closer?
qa.a: He paused and asked, 'This fine?'

qa.q: How can you tell Ramesh felt disappointed on Monday but still chose respect?
qa.a: He went quiet and kicked a pebble, which hints at disappointment, yet he thanked her for being honest instead of pushing.

qa.q: What made their talk about bigger steps a responsible one?
qa.a: They agreed any bigger step needs a real conversation first and proper protection, and that seeing a clinic together is nothing to be ashamed of, so both stay informed and safe.

qa.q: What would change for Yamini if Ramesh had argued on Monday?
qa.a: She might have felt pressured and less safe saying no later; his respect is what built the trust she describes on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a couple communicating boundaries, checking consent and planning responsibly, with trust growing over several days.

passage: Tushar, sit. You asked why I keep telling you boys to ask properly. When I was twenty-one, in Nagpur, I liked a girl from my college drama group. One evening after rehearsal I leaned in to kiss her, sure she wanted it because she'd been laughing at my jokes all week. She stepped back. Just one step. My face burned, and for a second I wanted to be angry, as if she owed me something. Luckily my mouth said, 'Sorry, I should have asked.' She looked relieved and said, 'I like you. Just slower.' We stayed friends for years. Laughing at a joke is not a yes, beta. A step back is a no. And whatever happens later in your life, you both talk first and keep each other safe.

qa.q: Where was the narrator studying when this happened?
qa.a: In Nagpur, as part of a college drama group.

qa.q: What did the narrator feel when the girl stepped back?
qa.a: Embarrassment, with a burning face, and a brief flash of anger as if she owed something, before choosing to apologise.

qa.q: What does the narrator want Tushar to take away from the story?
qa.a: That friendliness or laughter is not consent; Tushar should ask, treat a step back as a no, and talk openly before any intimacy.

qa.q: How might the girl have experienced the narrator's apology?
qa.a: She was relieved; the quick sorry showed her that her boundary was safe, which is why she could say she liked the narrator but wanted things slower.

grounding: An elder recalls learning at twenty-one that consent must be asked for and a boundary respected.

passage: The last metro left at 11:10, and it was 10:48 when Arvind said, "Stay tonight? It's raining anyway." Shalini's stomach tightened. They had been together four months, and she liked him, liked how he remembered her exam dates. But she wasn't ready to stay over, and she had hoped it wouldn't come up tonight, with the rain loud on the tin shade and no time to think. Her phone buzzed: Sarita, her roommate. "Home by 11:40? Shall I wait up?" Shalini took a breath. "I'm not ready for staying over. I like you. It's just not yet." Arvind was quiet for a second, then picked up the umbrella. "Okay. Thanks for telling me straight. Come, we'll run." They reached the platform at 11:06, soaked. She texted Sarita: "On the metro. He was sweet about it."

qa.q: What time did the last metro leave?
What was Shalini feeling when Arvind asked her to stay?
qa.a: Shalini felt anxious and pressured by the rain and the ticking clock, though she liked Arvind and simply wasn't ready.

qa.q: What could others learn from how both of them handled it?
qa.a: Shalini stated her boundary clearly and kindly, and Arvind accepted it at once, thanked her and helped her catch the metro.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the evening from her side?
qa.a: Sarita cared enough to offer to wait up, so reading 'He was sweet about it' would likely leave her relieved.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young woman states a boundary about staying over and her partner respects it.

passage: The student health centre on the third floor smelled of phenyl and the marigolds from someone's puja. Hansa had walked past its door twice before Zeenat linked arms and steered her in. "You said you wanted proper information, not internet rubbish," Zeenat whispered. Hansa's ears burned. She and Nikhil had been together a year and were talking about becoming intimate, and she wanted to understand protection and testing before anything happened. The nurse, reading glasses on a chain, didn't blink. She closed the door, gave Hansa leaflets, answered every question plainly, then asked one of her own: "Have you two talked about what each of you is comfortable with, and that either of you can stop anytime?" Hansa shook her head. "Start there," the nurse said. On the stairs down, Hansa laughed shakily. "That was the least awkward awkward thing ever."

qa.q: Where was the student health centre?
qa.a: On the third floor.

qa.q: What does Hansa walking past the door twice suggest?
qa.a: Hansa felt embarrassed and nervous about asking, even though she wanted proper information.

qa.q: What was wise about the nurse's question, and what should Hansa's next step be?
qa.a: It turned the focus to open talk with Nikhil about comfort and the right to stop anytime; Hansa's next step is that conversation.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel on the way down the stairs?
qa.a: Zeenat would likely feel relieved and glad she nudged Hansa in, seeing Hansa laugh after something so hard to start.

grounding: A young woman, supported by a friend, seeks reliable sexual-health information and is guided to talk about consent first.

passage:
"Okay, pretend I'm Sameer," Pooja said, flopping onto the hostel bed. "Go."
Mahima laughed nervously. "This is so silly."
"Last time you went quiet when you felt rushed, and then felt bad for days. So. Practice."
Mahima breathed out. "Sameer, I really like you. I want us to go slow. If I say stop, or go quiet, can you check with me?"
Pooja, in a deep voice: "What if I think you're just shy?"
"Then ask. Don't guess."
"Wow. Okay. That was clear." Pooja dropped the voice. "How do you feel?"
"Shaky. But like the words exist now."
"And if he sulks about it?"
Mahima picked at the blanket. "Then that tells me something about him, doesn't it?"
"It does." Pooja squeezed her hand. "You deserve someone who's glad you said it."

qa.q: Who did Pooja pretend to be?
qa.a: Sameer.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel after saying the words aloud?
qa.a: Mahima felt shaky but more confident, as if the words now existed for the real conversation.

qa.q: What makes Mahima's rehearsed sentence a good boundary statement?
qa.a: It is warm but clear: it says she likes him, wants to go slow, and asks him to check in rather than guess.

qa.q: Why might Pooja push Mahima to practise?
qa.a: Pooja saw Mahima feel bad for days after going quiet last time, so practising is a caring way to help her find her voice.

grounding: Two friends rehearse how to state a boundary and ask a partner to check for consent rather than guess.

passage:
When Ankita and I started dating in second year, I was nervous about everything. What if I said something wrong?
One evening, before things went further than kissing, she said, "Can we talk about what we're both okay with?" I felt awkward, but relieved too.
We talked about going slow. She said, "If either of us says stop, we stop, no sulking." I said the same.
Later, when we did decide to be more intimate, we went together to the campus health centre first. The nurse explained protection and testing without judging us.
I'm Naveen. Looking back, that first awkward talk was the most important one. It made everything after feel safe.

qa.q: Where did Naveen and Ankita go together before becoming more intimate?
qa.a: The campus health centre.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Ankita suggested talking about limits?
qa.a: Naveen felt awkward at first, but also relieved.

qa.q: What did Naveen and Ankita do that made their relationship safer?
qa.a: They discussed boundaries early, agreed that stop means stop, and got accurate information from the health centre.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Naveen agreed to stop without sulking?
qa.a: Ankita probably felt respected and safe with Naveen.

passage:
College health centre counsellor's note.
Jahnavi, second year, came in today with her friend Anjali for support. She said her boyfriend keeps pushing to go further physically, and says "if you loved me, you would." She has said no twice.
I told her she has every right to say no, and that love doesn't require proving anything. Consent must be freely given, every time. Pressure is not okay.
We talked about how to say it clearly, and what to do if he doesn't accept it. Anjali said she'd stay close. Jahnavi said she might end the relationship.
I gave her the centre's number and information on sexual health if she wants it later. Follow-up booked for next week. — Dr. Menon

qa.q: How many times has Jahnavi said no?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi likely feeling when she came in?
qa.a: Jahnavi was probably confused and pressured, maybe guilty for saying no.

qa.q: What did Dr. Menon do that supported Jahnavi?
qa.a: Dr. Menon affirmed her right to say no, named pressure as not okay, helped plan a clear response and booked a follow-up.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel supporting Jahnavi?
qa.a: Anjali likely feels protective and relieved that Jahnavi is getting good support.

grounding: A counsellor's note supports a young woman resisting sexual pressure from a partner.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Tonight Abhinav and I were at his place after the movie. We were kissing, and it was nice. Then he asked, "Is this okay? Do you want to stop or keep going?"
I realised I wanted to stop. I wasn't ready for more. I said so.
He said, "Okay. Thanks for telling me." He made tea, and we watched stupid videos until his roommate came home.
I'd always worried that saying no would ruin things. It didn't. It made me trust him more.
Also, we talked about how, if we ever do go further, we'll talk about protection first. That felt grown-up and a little embarrassing. Mostly grown-up.
— Dolma

qa.q: What did Abhinav make after Dolma wanted to stop?
qa.a: Tea.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling after saying no?
qa.a: Dolma felt relieved and more trusting, since saying no didn't ruin things.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do well to respect consent?
qa.a: He checked in by asking, accepted the answer calmly and kept things warm without pressure.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel after Dolma says she wants to stop?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel a little disappointed but respects Dolma, so he stays kind and relaxed.

grounding: In a diary a young adult experiences a partner checking consent and respecting a no.

passage:
Salma's wedding was fixed for after Eid, in their small town near Imphal, and she was scared to ask anyone the questions in her head. Her mother only said, "Everything will be fine."
Lalremsiami, her friend from college who now worked at the district health centre, came to visit. On the roof, drying chillies, Salma finally asked, "Is it wrong if I'm not ready on the first night?"
Lalremsiami put the tray down. "No. Marriage doesn't mean you stop being allowed to say no. Consent is still yours, every time."
She told Salma the health centre had a counsellor for newly married couples, where she and her husband could ask about family planning and protection privately, without anyone gossiping.
Salma let out a long breath. "Can I bring him to talk to her?"
"That's the best idea you've had all week."

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami work?
qa.a: At the district health centre.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling before she asked her question?
qa.a: Salma felt scared and alone with her questions, since her mother only said everything would be fine.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She stated clearly that consent stays Salma's even in marriage and pointed her to a private counsellor, giving facts and a safe place to ask.

qa.q: How might Salma's future husband see the counselling session?
qa.a: He might feel a little shy at first, but reassured that they can plan together openly.

grounding: Shows a young woman learning that consent continues within marriage and where to get private sexual-health guidance.

passage:
At a crowded house party in Mexico City, Camila noticed her friend Rania leaning hard against the wall, eyes half-closed. A guy Camila barely knew had his arm around her and was steering her toward a bedroom. "She's fine, she wants to lie down," he said.
Rania mumbled something that wasn't a word.
Camila stepped in front of them. "She can't decide anything like this. I'm taking her." Her heart was pounding. He shrugged, annoyed, and walked off.
Camila sat Rania on the stairs, got her water and called a friend with a car. She stayed with Rania until they were home and she was asleep on her side, then texted Rania's sister.
Next morning, Rania didn't remember much. When Camila told her, she went quiet, then said, "Thank you for not deciding I was fine."

qa.q: What did the guy say about Rania?
qa.a: He said, "She's fine, she wants to lie down."

qa.q: What does Camila's pounding heart suggest about how she felt stepping in?
qa.a: It suggests Camila felt scared and tense, but determined to protect her friend.

qa.q: Which of Camila's actions protected Rania, and why?
qa.a: Blocking the guy, getting Rania water and a safe ride home, staying with her and telling her sister, because someone that drunk can't give consent or keep herself safe.

qa.q: How might Rania see the night once she hears what happened?
qa.a: Rania likely feels shaken and deeply grateful, realising how vulnerable she was and that her friend protected her.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult recognising that an intoxicated person cannot consent and stepping in to protect her.

passage: The poster in the campus health centre's waiting room said, in big friendly letters, "Ask anything. It stays here." Disha sat under it with a folded list in her lap. Keerthana, her roommate, had come along without being asked. "You okay?" Keerthana whispered. Disha nodded. "Kabir and I talked last night. Properly. I told him I'm not ready for more yet, and that when I am, I want us both to be safe and sure." She twisted the paper. "I was scared he'd sulk." "Did he?" "He said, 'Thanks for telling me. We go at your pace, and you can change your mind anytime.'" Keerthana smiled. "That's the whole test, honestly." A nurse called Disha's name. She stood, took a breath, and walked in with her list, the questions she'd been too shy to search for alone.

qa.q: What did the poster in the waiting room say?
qa.a: It said, "Ask anything. It stays here."

qa.q: What was Disha worried about before talking to Kabir?
qa.a: She was scared he would sulk when she said she wasn't ready, and she still twists the paper nervously as she tells the story.

qa.q: Why is Disha's visit to the health centre a sensible step?
qa.a: She takes her questions to a trained person in a private setting instead of guessing, so any later choices are informed and safe.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Kabir's response?
qa.a: Keerthana sees it as a good sign, calling respect for Disha's pace and her right to change her mind the whole test of a partner.

grounding: Shows a young woman stating a boundary, a partner respecting consent, and her seeking reliable sexual health information.
